article_title: Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review.
citation: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review. F1000Research 9:164. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.21858.1
title: The IHC Key Concepts Framework: principles for evaluating the trustworthiness of treatment claims, organised as concepts, competences, and dispositions
description: The Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework is a structure of concepts, competences, and dispositions for evaluating the trustworthiness of claims about treatment effects and for making informed health choices. The article states that "The concepts are principles for evaluating the trustworthiness of treatment claims and the evidence used to support these, and for making informed choices." The current (2019) version includes 49 concepts in three groups (Claims, Comparisons, Choices), 20 competences in four groups, and 16 dispositions in four groups, and serves as a starting point for teachers, journalists, researchers and other intermediaries developing learning resources.
requirements: To be usable as a framework, sources must include a description of the purpose, a list of elements, and definitions of key terms, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The framework targets treatment (intervention) claims about health, though people in other fields have found the concepts relevant for assessing claims about other types of interventions
target_learners: teachers, journalists, researchers and other intermediaries
target_learning_goals: assessing the trustworthiness of treatment claims
examples: The 2019 framework's Table 1 organises concepts under Claims, Comparisons, and Choices; Table 2 lists competences such as recognising unfair treatment comparisons; Table 3 lists dispositions such as questioning the basis for treatment claims
key_sources: Oxman Andrew D., García Laura Martínez. (2020). Comparison of the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts Framework to other frameworks relevant to teaching and learning how to think critically about health claims and choices: a systematic review. F1000Research 9:164. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.21858.1

article_title: Integrating iHEC into standardized residency training for chronic disease management: a structural equation analysis of competency outcomes via digital health platforms.
citation: Xie Dili, Sun Xuechun, Guo Jianshu, Liu Peng, Yang Junling, Zhong Ping. (2026). Integrating iHEC into standardized residency training for chronic disease management: a structural equation analysis of competency outcomes via digital health platforms. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1926948
title: iHEC (Intelligent Hypertension Excellence Centers) digital platform used as an interactive residency learning environment
description: The iHEC platform, launched by the China Hypertension Alliance and led by the Shanghai Institute of Hypertension, uses "Bluetooth, wireless remote networking, and wide-area network technologies" to support hypertension diagnosis and management. In this study it was repurposed as a teaching environment: residents managed real-time digitized patient profiles, performed dynamic blood pressure trajectory monitoring, used embedded clinical decision-support systems, and constructed chronic disease management plans, reviewing a minimum of 15 authentic digital hypertension cases per rotation (average 18.4 ± 2.6), with bi-weekly supervisor review and a 30-min weekly structured debrief.
requirements: Residents required faculty orientation (a mandatory 4-h orientation on platform functionality and debriefing rubrics) and weekly audits of platform usage logs to ensure intervention fidelity
constraints: Evaluated in a single geriatric cardiology department within a tertiary academic hospital; generalizability to other specialties or institutions with different digital infrastructure requires further validation
target_learners: resident physicians in standardized residency training (geriatric cardiology rotation)
target_learning_goals: hypertension and chronic disease management competency
examples: During the 4-week rotation, iHEC cohort residents managed real-time digitized patient profiles and reviewed an average of 18.4 ± 2.6 digital hypertension cases with bi-weekly structured online feedback
